lab.name: Wild & Heritage Species
lab.description: Non-Saccharomyces and wild alcohol-producing microbes, catalogued at the species level. A species does not have a fermentation temperature range — a commercial strain does — so numeric specs here are null unless a named datasheet for a named product supplies them, in which case the product is named in the entry. Everything else is described in prose with the figure attributed to whoever published it.

attribution: Each entry cites one document, recorded in sourceId/sourceUrl and catalogued in data/sources/registry.json. Numeric fields are populated only from vendor technical data sheets for specific products; literature-derived figures are stated in prose with the original study attributed, because the published values disagree with each other and collapsing them into a single number would misrepresent them.

strains.name: Brettanomyces bruxellensis (species)
strains.description: The classic 'Brett' of Belgian sour and wild ales, and the organism behind Brett character in wine. The Maltose Falcons' club guide places its origin in Brussels and describes it as producing a medium amount of the earthy funk associated with Brett — between the softer claussenii and the much bigger lambicus.
strains.optimalPitchNote: Slow — plan in months, not weeks. All numeric specs are null: an earlier version of this record claimed 85-100% attenuation, 16-29 °C and 12% alcohol tolerance while citing a Wikipedia page on the genus, which supports none of those numbers. Attenuation in particular is strain-dependent and depends on how much dextrin the primary yeast left behind.
strains.sourceNote: Supports: Brussels origin, medium earthy funk, position relative to the other Brett species. Does not support: attenuation, temperature, flocculation, alcohol tolerance — all null.

strains.name: Lachancea thermotolerans (as WildBrew Philly Sour)
strains.description: A yeast that produces both lactic acid and ethanol, souring and fermenting in one step with no bacteria involved. The figures here are the published specification for Lallemand's WildBrew Philly Sour, a pure active dried L. thermotolerans strain — not species-wide values. Its datasheet gives 74-82% attenuation, 20-30 °C (optimal 25-30 °C), high flocculation, 9% ABV tolerance, 50-150 g/hL, and fermentation completable in ten days at 20 °C. The strain is POF negative, diastaticus negative and killer negative.
strains.flavorNotes: Sour, red apple, stone fruit, notably peach (WildBrew Philly Sour datasheet descriptors).
strains.optimalPitchNote: Datasheet pitching rate is 50-150 g/hL, viability at least 1x10^9 CFU/g. Lower temperatures within the 20-25 °C band call for the higher end of that rate. The pH 3.2-3.5 and 0.1-0.4% lactic acid figures the datasheet quotes apply to Lallemand's standard-conditions wort, so treat them as indicative rather than a promise about your wort. An earlier version of this record claimed 70-82% attenuation, 17-28 °C, medium flocculation and 10% tolerance — every one of those four was wrong against the datasheet.
strains.sourceNote: Supports: every numeric field above, for this product. Does not support: species-wide behaviour of L. thermotolerans, or wine applications — the datasheet is a brewing document.

strains.name: Torulaspora delbrueckii (species)
strains.description: A non-Saccharomyces yeast of established interest both as a pure brewing starter and, more commonly, in wine co-fermentation. Michel et al.'s review of pure non-Saccharomyces starter cultures covers it among the species of brewing interest; in winemaking its documented value is lower volatile acidity and increased aromatic contribution when inoculated sequentially before Saccharomyces.
strains.flavorNotes: Aromatic contribution with low volatile acidity; the specific ester profile depends heavily on strain and on whether it is used pure or sequentially.
strains.optimalPitchNote: In wine it is normally inoculated first and followed by Saccharomyces, which is where the volatile-acidity benefit comes from; used entirely alone it will usually stick before a wine ferments dry. Numeric specs are null — the cited review does not publish species-level temperature, attenuation or alcohol-tolerance ranges, and the previous version of this record asserted 60-78% attenuation, 18-28 °C and 9% tolerance on the strength of a Wikipedia species page.
strains.sourceNote: Supports: standing as a non-Saccharomyces brewing starter, and the low-volatile-acidity/aromatic role in sequential wine fermentation. Does not support: any numeric range — all null. Verification is metadata-only (abstract and search summaries, not full text).

strains.name: Kluyveromyces marxianus (species)
strains.description: A fast-growing, genuinely thermotolerant yeast that assimilates and ferments lactose, which most brewing yeast cannot — hence its interest for whey and dairy-based ferments. Fonseca et al.'s review reports maximum growth temperature variously as 47 °C (Anderson et al. 1986), 49 °C (Hughes et al. 1984) and 52 °C (Banat et al. 1992), and ethanol production above 40 °C. Two findings from the same review matter more for anyone thinking of pitching it: its ethanol tolerance is LOWER than that of S. cerevisiae, and it is Crabtree-negative and cannot grow under strictly anaerobic conditions, with ethanol formation almost exclusively tied to oxygen availability.
strains.flavorNotes: Fruity and ester-rich; will ferment milk sugar.
strains.optimalPitchNote: Not a drop-in replacement for a brewing yeast. Because it cannot grow strictly anaerobically and its ethanol formation is oxygen-linked, a conventional sealed, oxygen-free fermentation is the wrong environment for it. No numeric fields are populated: the published maximum growth temperatures disagree (47/49/52 °C) and are growth limits rather than recommended fermentation ranges, so they are reported above with their attributions instead of being averaged into a fake range. The alcohol tolerance is null and deliberately so — an earlier version of this record claimed 10%, which is the figure reported for strains after roughly 100 days of directed adaptive evolution, not a native specification, and it pointed in the opposite direction to what the literature actually says. That earlier version also listed 'Bioethanol' as a recommended style, which is an industrial application and not a drink.
strains.sourceNote: Supports: lactose assimilation and fermentation, thermotolerance with the three attributed maxima, ethanol production above 40 °C, lower ethanol tolerance than S. cerevisiae, Crabtree-negative character, inability to grow strictly anaerobically. Does not support: any single alcohol-tolerance number, attenuation, flocculation, or a recommended fermentation temperature range — all null.

strains.name: Saccharomycodes ludwigii (species)
strains.description: A maltose- and maltotriose-negative yeast: it will not ferment the main wort sugars, so it produces very little alcohol while still generating fermentation aroma. Michel et al.'s review notes that it is the most studied yeast for low- and non-alcoholic beer and that alcohol-free beer is already produced industrially with it, which is what makes it interesting — the low alcohol comes from what the yeast cannot eat rather than from stripping alcohol back out afterwards.
strains.flavorNotes: Fermentation-derived aroma with very little alcohol; the review's point is that the flavours are desirable rather than merely tolerable.
strains.optimalPitchNote: The approach works because the sugars are left behind, which means the finished beer is sweet and full of fermentable material — it is microbiologically vulnerable and needs the same care as any low-alcohol product. Numeric specs are null; the cited review does not publish species-level ranges.
strains.sourceNote: Supports: maltose- and maltotriose-negative character, resulting low alcohol with desirable flavour, industrial use for alcohol-free beer. Does not support: temperature, attenuation, flocculation, alcohol tolerance — all null. Verification is metadata-only.
